Classical boundary element methods for electromagnetic scattering suffer from low-frequency breakdown, losing stability as frequency approaches zero.
The scattering problem is modeled by the second-order curl-curl equation for the electric field with angular frequency ω > 0.
The boundary condition on the perfect electric conductor is a Dirichlet condition prescribing the tangential electric field trace.
The Silver–Müller radiation condition ensures proper decay of scattered fields at infinity.
Energy spaces H(curl) and H(div) are used to define weak solutions with square-integrable fields and their derivatives.
Trace spaces H^{1/2} with div and curl regularity characterize the boundary values of electromagnetic fields.
The continuity equation links the surface delta distributions of the normal electric field and tangential magnetic field traces.
The stabilized formulation incorporates the continuity equation explicitly to prevent low-frequency instability.
For ω = 0, the electric field reduces to an electrostatic field, and the stabilized formulation remains valid.
The paper proves that the classical Maxwell system in distributional form leads to boundary integral equations with additional surface terms.
Integration by parts formulas are extended to energy spaces to handle boundary traces rigorously.
The paper uses Lipschitz polyhedral domains to model scatterer boundaries, allowing for realistic geometries.
The normal and tangential traces are defined as limits of test functions approaching the boundary from the exterior domain.
The stabilized boundary element method is verified by numerical examples showing robustness for all frequencies ω > 0.
The mathematical theory relies on recent results about the regularity and trace characterization of vector fields on Lipschitz boundaries.
The paper provides explicit formulas for the weak enforcement of Maxwell's equations in distributional sense.
The classical boundary element formulation fails to impose the Gauss law sufficiently at low frequencies.
The stabilized formulation ensures uniform stability and convergence of the numerical solution across frequencies.
The paper includes a detailed functional analytic framework for the Maxwell scattering problem.
The continuity equation for the surface delta distributions holds as h(NE, ∇φ) = ω² h(nE, φ) for test functions φ.
